Wellspring
WEL-spring
n.
Old English compound: wella (well, source of water, spring) + spring (the source or origin of a stream); denoting the original source or origin of a flowing supply. In Scripture, wellspring translates Hebrew māqôr (spring, source; also rendered “fountain”) and Greek pēgē (spring, source; used in John 4:14 and Rev 21:6 of the water of life). The image is consistently applied to the divine life flowing from God and given freely to those who thirst.

Biblical Definition

Wellspring is the biblical image of God Himself as the inexhaustible, originating source of all life, light, and saving grace — and of Christ and the Spirit as the channels through which that living source flows into the redeemed. The foundational declaration is Psalm 36:9: “For with thee is the fountain of life: in thy light shall we see light.” God is the wellspring of life in the absolute sense: He does not receive life from any source outside Himself but is the origin from which all life flows. Proverbs 4:23 turns the image pastoral and inward: “Above all else, guard your heart, for it is the wellspring of life” — the spiritual centre of the person, renewed by grace, becomes itself a wellspring when the heart is rightly ordered toward God. Isaiah 55:1 opens the great invitation: “Ho! Everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and you who have no money, come, buy and eat.” The wellspring requires nothing from those who drink; it gives freely to all who will come. Christ expands this in John 7:38: “Whoever believes in Me — as the Scripture has said — 'Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.'” The believer who has drunk from the divine wellspring becomes a conduit of the same living water to others. Revelation 22:1 shows the consummation: “a river of the water of life, clear as crystal — coming from the throne of God and of the Lamb.” The eschatological city has no reservoir; it has a wellspring that is the eternal God Himself, flowing without interruption to all who thirst, world without end.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a wellspring as the fountain-head or primary source of a stream; in theological application, the wellspring of all life is God Himself — the One who has life in Himself and gives it freely to those who come to Him in Christ.

expand to see more

WELLSPRING, n. [well and spring.] The fountain-head; the source of a spring or stream; the original source from which anything proceeds in abundance. Webster (1828) gives the example of a wellspring of pleasure, indicating an inexhaustible originating supply.

In Scripture, wellspring and fountain (“fountain of life,” Ps 36:9; “fountain of living waters,” Jer 2:13) are used interchangeably for God as the originating source of all good. The image is theologically charged: a fountain supplies without being diminished, flows without ceasing, and asks nothing of those who drink from it. God's grace is a wellspring, not a reservoir — it does not run low.

Key Scripture

Psalm 36:9 — "For with thee is the fountain of life: in thy light shall we see light."

John 7:38 — "He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water."

Isaiah 55:1 — "Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price."

Revelation 22:1 — "And he shewed me a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb."

Modern Corruption

Liberal theology replaces the divine wellspring with human religious impulse and social solidarity as the sources of spiritual life; New Age spirituality locates the wellspring within the autonomous self rather than in the triune God; prosperity theology treats the wellspring as a reward for material faith-steps rather than a free gift of grace.

expand to see more

Liberal Protestant theology, following Schleiermacher, relocates the source of spiritual life from the triune God to the human religious consciousness — the “sense and taste for the Infinite” within. On this account, the wellspring is internal and universal: every human being has access to divine life through their own religious depth. This inverts Ps 36:9. The fountain of life is “with You” — with God, external to the creature, accessible only by approach to the One who has life in Himself. Jeremiah named the great apostasy precisely: Israel had “forsaken Me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves — broken cisterns that can hold no water” (Jer 2:13). The self as wellspring is a broken cistern, not a living spring.

New Age spirituality speaks of “tapping into” universal life-force energy, the divine spark within, or the higher self as the source of renewal and vitality. The imagery borrows the wellspring metaphor while severing it from the personal God who alone possesses life in Himself (John 5:26). Christ's promise in John 7:38 does not say “out of his heart will flow rivers of living water” as an autonomous achievement of the spiritually cultivated self; John 7:39 explains that this is the Spirit given to those who believe in Christ. The wellspring within the believer is the Holy Spirit — a Person, not a force — and He flows from the Father and the Son, not from human spiritual development.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The wellspring image runs through the entire biblical canon from Eden's river to the crystal river of Revelation 22, unifying the theology of divine life, the gift of the Spirit, and the eschatological restoration of all that sin has parched and dried.

expand to see more

Hebrew māqôr — spring, source, fountain; used in Ps 36:9 (“fountain of life”) and Prov 13:14 (“fountain of life”); often rendered “wellspring” in older English translations.

Hebrew mayin chayyīm — living waters; water from a flowing spring (as opposed to a cistern), used in Levitical purity law and as a prophetic image of divine grace (Jer 2:13; 17:13; Zech 14:8).

Greek pēgē — spring, source of water; used in John 4:14 (“a spring of water welling up to eternal life”), Rev 7:17 (“springs of living water”), and Rev 21:6 (“the spring of the water of life”).

Genesis 2:10 — a river flows out of Eden to water the garden; the beginning of the biblical wellspring pattern, which Ezekiel 47 and Revelation 22 bring to eschatological fulfilment.

Revelation 22:1–2 — the river of the water of life proceeding from the throne of God and the Lamb; the eschatological wellspring that makes the new creation perpetually fruitful and the nations perpetually healed.

Usage

"Psalm 36:9 grounds the wellspring image in the divine aseity: God has life in Himself and is therefore the only inexhaustible source of life for creatures who have it derivatively. To draw life from any other source is to draw from a well that will run dry."

"Christ's promise in John 7:38 turns the believer into a secondary wellspring: the Spirit given to those who believe in Christ flows outward to others as “rivers of living water” — not the believer's own spiritual vitality but the overflow of the Spirit who indwells them."

"Isaiah 55:1's great invitation frames the wellspring as entirely free and unconditional: “without money and without price.” The one qualification for drinking from the divine wellspring is thirst — the recognition of one's own spiritual need — which grace itself creates in the hearts of the elect."
